lede: A plant leaks water all day long. It evaporates inside the leaf and drifts out through the stomata, and the pull that replaces it drags water all the way up from the roots. A potometer is how you measure it.
can: Define transpiration with all three stages, naming the air spaces and the stomata.
Say which way each of the five factors moves the rate, and explain why.
Turn potometer readings into a rate and a percentage change, with units.

text: Transpiration, the potometer and uses of water

md: A sunflower drinks about a litre of water on a hot day, and almost none of it stays. It evaporates out of the leaves as invisible vapour. That steady leak has a name — transpiration — and it is what pulls water up from the roots.

md:
**1. Evaporation** from the surfaces of the **mesophyll cells**.
**2. Diffusion through the air spaces** between the spongy cells.
**3. Out through the stomata**, because there is more vapour inside the leaf than outside.

What is lost is replaced by water pulled up the **xylem**, which is why transpiration and water uptake go together.

prompt: Water vapour crosses the air spaces and then leaves the leaf through the ______.
explain: Stomata. Both the air spaces and the stomata are worth a mark of their own, so name them both.

title: Why one idea explains all five
md:
Vapour leaves because there is **more of it inside the leaf than outside**. Anything that makes that difference bigger speeds transpiration up; anything that makes it smaller slows it down.

Wind sweeps the vapour away, so the difference grows. Warmth makes more vapour inside, so the difference grows. Humid air is already full of vapour, so the difference shrinks — and that is why humidity is the odd one out.

prompt: Which factor is the only one that makes the rate go DOWN as it increases?
explain: Humidity. Damp air outside means a smaller difference in water vapour concentration, so the vapour diffuses out more slowly.

md:
Every joint is **airtight** and the whole tube is full of water, so every cubic millimetre the shoot takes up has to be drawn in at the open end — and the bubble is carried along with it. How far the bubble travels **is** how much water the shoot has taken up.

To **reset** it, open the **tap on the reservoir**: water runs in and pushes the bubble back to the start. Some potometers use a syringe, and you push the plunger.

prompt: Which way does the bubble move while the shoot is taking up water?
explain: Towards the shoot. The bubble follows the water being drawn in to replace what the leaves lost.

title: Worked example: 'The bubble moved from 10 mm to 42 mm in 20 minutes. Calculate the rate. [2]'
md:
**Step 1 — find the distance.** 42 − 10 = **32 mm**. The bubble did not start at zero, so the subtraction is a mark of its own.
**Step 2 — divide by the time.** 32 ÷ 20 = **1.6 mm per minute**. A rate is always an amount per unit of time, and the unit falls straight out of the division.

prompt: Your turn for run C: the bubble went from 10 mm to 50 mm in 20 minutes. Give the rate in mm per minute.

title: GCSE Biology Revision "Transpiration"
why: A short second pass over the same factors, now that you have the mechanism.

md:
From run A to run B the rate rose from 1.6 to 2.4 mm per minute — an increase of 0.8. As a percentage of what you started with:

0.8 ÷ 1.6 × 100 = **50.0%**

And when a question says *use data to explain*, the figures themselves are the marks.

prompt: In a percentage increase, what do you divide the increase by?
explain: The original. Dividing by the new value is the commonest slip in this calculation, in every subject.

md:
At midday the light is brightest and the air warmest, so the stomata are wide open for photosynthesis and the vapour leaves fast. Overnight the stomata close and uptake almost stops.

Read this axis carefully: **midnight appears twice and midday once**, so a time answer has to say which one you mean.

prompt: Why is water uptake greatest at midday?
options: Light and temperature are highest, so the stomata are open and the vapour leaves fastest
The plant is photosynthesising, so it makes more water
The roots take up water only during daylight
answer: Light and temperature are highest, so the stomata are open and the vapour leaves fastest
explain: The stomata are the link: open for photosynthesis, and losing water at the same time.

text: 7. Two more ways to measure, and what the water is for

title: Diffusion
attribution: Simulation by PhET Interactive Simulations, University of Colorado Boulder, licensed under CC BY-NC 4.0 (https://phet.colorado.edu)
task: Crowd one side of the divider, remove it, and watch the net movement. Then say in one sentence why water vapour leaves a leaf faster on a windy day, using the word difference.

md:
A **weight potometer** stands the whole apparatus on a balance: the mass lost is the water taken up, and a layer of oil stops anything evaporating from the flask. Ours fell from 186.50 g to 184.70 g in 30 minutes. The **washing-line method** weighs cut leaves, hangs them up and weighs them again.

The water a plant keeps has four uses: **support**, **transport**, **transpiration** and **photosynthesis**.

prompt: How much mass did the weight potometer lose, in grams? (186.50 g down to 184.70 g.)
explain: 186.50 − 184.70 = 1.80 g, which is the water the shoot took up.

title: You can now…

md:
Trace the water from the soil to the air.
Name five factors that change the rate, and say which way each moves it.
Describe how a potometer measures that rate.
Compare two runs using numbers from the data.

The potometer question runs to about nine marks with the same bones every time: a structure to name, two more to name, a relationship to state, a graph to complete, another factor, and the bubble for three. In Booklet B it grows a calculation and a *use data to explain* part. Stuck: say which way the bubble moves, and why.
